name: Presidential proclamation of February 10, 1890 reserving the Cheyenne River agency and school lands (Royce 711)
aka: Proclamation opening the ceded Great Sioux Reservation lands, February 10, 1890 (in part)
promises: Not a treaty. By the proclamation the President reserved a tract on the Missouri around the mouth of the Cheyenne River, including the school buildings, about three miles south of the river and five and a half miles west (Royce).
today: The 1889 Act came into force by proclamation on February 10, 1890 (105 Ct. Cl. 725); its taking is recorded under cession-1889-03-02-sioux and the Cheyenne River reservation under cession-1889-03-02-sioux-cheyenne-river. The Cheyenne River Sioux history says the agency had to move because ceded land left it outside the new boundary.

nationVoice.summary: The history the Tribe publishes says the 1889 Act set the reservation boundaries and that the agency town had to move because it fell outside them.

sources.title: Royce, Indian Land Cessions in the United States (18th Annual Report, Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899), schedule p. 938, Cheyenne River Sioux, Feb. 10, 1890
Sioux Tribe of Indians v. United States, 105 Ct. Cl. 725 (1946), Nos. C-531 (18) to (24)
sources.publisher: Caselaw Access Project, Harvard Law School

openQuestions: Royce 711 is land reserved for the Sioux, not taken. No finding about this tract was found. Whether the old agency tract was later restored to the public domain, and on what terms, was not traced.
The proclamation text at 26 Stat. 1554 was read only through Royce.
